overview: Sous-Storefront is a server-rendered React e-commerce storefront that lets shoppers browse products by category, manage a cart, and complete a simulated checkout. Built on React Router v7 with TanStack Query for data fetching, it runs as a Node 20 Alpine Docker container serving SSR pages that hydrate into a fully interactive SPA. All product data comes from the public DummyJSON API; cart and theme preferences persist in browser localStorage via Zustand stores.
structure_narrative: The system spans three runtime boundaries. The **server** handles SSR rendering and build-time prerendering -- route loaders prefetch data from DummyJSON, dehydrate TanStack Query caches, and ship HTML to the browser. The **browser** receives hydrated pages and takes over with client-side routing, infinite scroll pagination, cart management, and theme toggling. The **external** boundary includes the DummyJSON REST API (the sole data source) and browser-native APIs (localStorage for persistence, DOM for theme application). This is a thin-client architecture: there is no backend of its own, no database, and no authentication. The server is a rendering layer, not an application server.

data_flows.name: SSR Prefetch & Hydration
data_flows.narrative: When a shopper first navigates to the storefront, the request hits the Node server where react-router-serve picks the matching route. The **root-layout-loader** fires first, creating a fresh QueryClient and calling prefetchQuery with **categories-query** options -- this fetches the full category list from **dummyjson** via the **api-client**. For the home page, the **home-loader** goes further: it awaits the categories, then calls prefetchInfiniteQuery on **category-sections-query** to warm the first page (4 categories, 4 products each). The **products-loader** does the same for /products, prefetching 8 products. Each loader then dehydrates the QueryClient into serialized state and passes it through useLoaderData. On the client, **app-root** wraps everything in QueryClientProvider, and each route's HydrationBoundary rehydrates the cache -- so TanStack Query hooks read from warm cache on first render, avoiding a flash of loading state. This is the core performance story: the server does the expensive API round-trips to DummyJSON, and the browser picks up where the server left off.

steps.action: wraps in QueryClientProvider, HydrationBoundary rehydrates cache

data_flows.name: Client-Side Browsing
data_flows.narrative: Once hydrated, the shopper browses entirely client-side. On the home page, **home-page** uses an intersection observer to detect when the user scrolls near the bottom, triggering fetchNextPage on **category-sections-query** -- which pages through categories in batches of 4 via **api-client** to **dummyjson**. Each batch loads with an (unfortunate) artificial 800ms delay baked into the query function. On /products, **products-page** uses **products-query** with a Load more button for manual pagination, 8 products at a time. The **nav-menu** drawer reads **categories-query** (already warm from SSR) to list all browsable categories, and clicking one triggers a client-side route transition to /products/:category. The entire browsing experience stays within TanStack Query's cache -- re-visiting a category page finds warm data rather than re-fetching.

data_flows.name: Cart Lifecycle
data_flows.narrative: When Sarah finds a product she likes, she clicks Add to cart on a **product-card**. The card's onAddToCart callback calls addItem on the **cart-store**, which upserts the product into the items array (incrementing quantity if already present) and recomputes the total via reduce. A sonner toast confirms the action. The **cart-drawer** in the header reactively reflects the new state -- showing the item with quantity controls. Sarah can increment, decrement, or remove items directly in the drawer. Clicking Checkout navigates to **checkout-page**, which runs a clientLoader guard: if the cart is empty, it redirects to **products-page**. The checkout two-column layout renders **order-summary** (reading cart items and computing subtotal + 20% VAT) alongside **shipping-form** and **payment-form**. When Sarah submits, the clientAction simulates order processing with a 1-second delay, then calls clear() on **cart-store**, sets the successfulOrder flag, and redirects to **success-page**. The success page's clientLoader checks that flag (redirecting away if absent), clears it, and fires a confetti animation. Throughout this entire flow, **cart-store** persists to **localstorage** via Zustand's persist middleware, so cart state survives page refreshes.

steps.action: clientLoader guard checks cart, clientAction simulates order

data_flows.name: Theme Toggle
data_flows.narrative: When the page first loads, **app-root** runs a useEffect that imperatively reads the **theme-store** (outside React's render cycle to avoid hydration mismatch) and applies the persisted dark or light class to document.documentElement. When a shopper clicks the **theme-toggle** button, it calls setTheme on **theme-store**, which does two things simultaneously: updates the Zustand state (triggering re-renders of any subscribers like the Sonner Toaster) and directly mutates the **dom** classList for instant CSS variable switching -- no React re-render needed for the visual change. The store's persist middleware writes the preference to **localstorage**, so returning visitors see their chosen theme immediately.

data_flows.name: Route Navigation
data_flows.narrative: React Router v7 organizes the app into a nested route tree. **app-root** renders an Outlet that, for / and /products paths, resolves to **root-layout** -- which provides the shared **header** with nav, cart, and theme controls. For /checkout and /success, the Outlet bypasses **root-layout** entirely, rendering standalone pages without the header (a deliberate design choice: checkout is a focused flow). Within **root-layout**, a second Outlet renders either **home-page** (as index) or **products-page** (as child). Client-side guards on **checkout-page** and **success-page** use clientLoader to enforce state preconditions: checkout requires a non-empty cart, success requires the successfulOrder flag. Both redirect to **products-page** when their guard fails.

data_flows.name: E2E Test Coverage
data_flows.narrative: Playwright tests validate the two critical user journeys. **test-products** covers browsing: it verifies product display by category (checking breadcrumb and card anatomy), tests the add-to-cart flow (toast notification, **cart-drawer** opening, item verification), and validates category navigation via the **nav-menu** drawer. **test-checkout** covers the full purchase path: starting from **products-page**, it adds a product, opens the **cart-drawer**, navigates to **checkout-page**, fills both **shipping-form** and **payment-form**, submits the order, and verifies the **success-page** renders correctly. These 4 tests run across chromium, firefox, and webkit via GitHub Actions CI on every push.

steps.action: verifies product display and cart interaction

state.name: Cart Store
state.narrative: Cart state lives in **cart-store**, a Zustand store persisted to **localstorage** under the key cart-storage. This is a deliberate trade-off: there is no server-side cart, so cart contents are device-local and ephemeral. The store holds an items array (product + quantity pairs), a computed total (recomputed via reduce on every mutation -- a minor inefficiency noted as tech debt), and a successfulOrder boolean flag that bridges the checkout-to-success transition. Five actions mutate state: addItem performs upsert (insert or increment), removeItem/incrementItem/decrementItem modify quantities, and clear resets everything. The successfulOrder flag is a coordination mechanism: **checkout-page** sets it before redirecting, and **success-page** reads and clears it as a one-time gate.
state.purpose: source-of-truth for cart contents and checkout coordination

state.name: Theme Store
state.narrative: Theme preference lives in **theme-store**, also Zustand-persisted to **localstorage** (key: theme-storage). The store tracks a single value: dark, light, or system. The interesting design choice is dual-write: setTheme both updates Zustand state (for React subscribers) and directly mutates **dom** classList on documentElement. This avoids a flash of wrong theme during React's render cycle. **app-root** reads the store imperatively (not via hook) on mount to apply the initial class, and the Sonner **ui-primitives** Toaster subscribes reactively for toast theming.

state.name: TanStack Query Cache
state.narrative: The query cache is the third state container, managed by TanStack Query rather than Zustand. **app-root** creates a fresh QueryClient per request (important for SSR -- shared clients would leak state between users). SSR loaders populate it via prefetchQuery/prefetchInfiniteQuery, and HydrationBoundary transfers that state to the client. Once hydrated, the cache governs staleness, refetching, and garbage collection. Three query families share the cache: **categories-query** (warm across most pages), **category-sections-query** (home page infinite scroll), and **products-query** (products page infinite scroll). Because the cache is in-memory and per-tab, navigating between categories reuses cached data without re-fetching -- but closing the tab loses everything.
state.purpose: server-state cache for DummyJSON API data

failure_modes.narrative: When the DummyJSON API goes down or starts returning 5xx errors, the entire storefront breaks. The **api-client** has no retry policy, no timeout, and no circuit breaker. On the server side, **root-layout-loader**, **home-loader**, and **products-loader** will hang indefinitely waiting for a response -- blocking SSR and making the site unresponsive. On the client side, TanStack Query's default retry (3 attempts) provides some resilience for subsequent fetches, but the initial SSR-blocking request has no such protection. There is no fallback UI: error boundaries exist in **app-root** but are generic 404/error displays, not graceful degradation. The fix requires three changes: ky timeout configuration (e.g., 5s), ky retry for transient failures, and per-route error boundaries with meaningful error states.

cascade.effect: nav menu has no categories to display

detection: No structured logging for request failures
recovery: Requires DummyJSON to recover -- no fallback data source
Browser hard refresh after API recovers

failure_modes.narrative: If **localstorage** is full or unavailable (private browsing in some browsers, storage quota exceeded), the Zustand persist middleware in **cart-store** and **theme-store** silently fails to write. The stores still function in-memory for the session, but cart contents and theme preference are lost on page refresh. This is a graceful degradation by default -- Zustand's persist middleware catches storage errors -- but the user gets no indication that their cart won't survive a refresh.

cascade.effect: cart state not persisted across refreshes

detection: No monitoring -- silent failure by design
recovery: Stores recover automatically when storage becomes available

failure_modes.narrative: The **shipping-form** and **payment-form** use only HTML required attributes for validation -- no schema validation via Zod or similar. The **checkout-page** clientAction trusts whatever the browser submits. In the current demo this is harmless (the backend is simulated), but it means any future real backend integration inherits unvalidated input. A malicious or buggy form submission could send malformed data that a real payment processor would reject or, worse, process incorrectly.

cascade.effect: accepts any non-empty string as email, postal code, etc.
accepts any non-empty string as card number, CVV

detection: No server-side validation exists to catch bad input
recovery: Add Zod schema validation before clientAction processes the form

failure_modes.narrative: DummyJSON responds slowly but does not error. The **home-loader** makes multiple sequential API calls (categories first, then 4 product fetches for the first page of category sections), and the artificial 800ms delay in **category-sections-query** compounds the problem. Without a timeout, a slow DummyJSON response (say 10s per request) means the home page SSR takes 40+ seconds. The user sees a blank page (or browser timeout) with no indication of progress. The **products-loader** is less affected (single query) but still blocks indefinitely.
